text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes · 01 of 3 One Front Door How work moves through a team of AI agents, and why I only talk to one of them. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 I run two businesses with nine AI agents. I talk to one of them. That one is called AXIOM. Everything I need goes to it first: a reel that needs fixing, a client's meal plan, a sales follow-up, a bug in the coaching app. AXIOM decides who does the work, writes the job down, checks the result, and brings one answer back to me. This note is about why it's built that way. The problem with many doors Before October 11, I opened whichever agent fit the job. The app builder for code. A content agent for reels. A sales agent for DMs. Each one kept its own notes. Each one knew its slice. None of them knew what the others had done that day. When two jobs touched each other, I was the only one who could see it. I was carrying the whole picture in my head and passing it between agents by hand. That is the job I built the system to take off me. More agents made it worse, not better. The front door So the rule changed. One agent receives everything. It has four jobs: Receive. I say what I want in plain English. I don't pick a model or a folder. Route. AXIOM decides which specialist fits and writes the job as a card on a shared board. Verify. When the specialist says it's done, AXIOM checks the work itself before it reaches me. Report. I get one answer, not nine. The specialists don't come to me. They report to AXIOM. One request goes in, one answer comes out. Specialists never report to the owner directly; their "done" is checked by AXIOM before it counts. Every job is a card Each card gets a short code: a letter for the part of the business and the next number in that series. A is Axiom, P is PKFIT coaching, C is content, H is operations. Codes are never reused, so "C1" means one thing forever. Here is a real one from October 14. A client's stage reel had the wrong placings on its end card. AXIOM opened C1, gave it to the operations agent with the correct results, and waited. When the agent reported back, AXIOM didn't take its word for it. It pulled the frame at 33.5 seconds and read the text, checked the length and audio level, and confirmed the new file had landed in the shared folder. Then it told me the reel was ready. I never opened the operations agent. I didn't need to know it existed. Specialists stay narrow A front door only works if what's behind it is boring and specific. The app builder writes and tests code. It doesn't put anything live. The code reviewer reads code and returns a verdict. It doesn't write any. The builder never judges its own work. Narrow roles are easier to trust, because when something goes wrong there are only a few places it could have come from. Nothing ends quietly Every conversation with any agent ends one of two ways: a written handoff the next session can pick up, or one line in a shared log. From October 11 to 14, that log took 116 entries. And an agent saying "done" does not close anything. AXIOM closes a job only after it has checked the result against something real: the file, the page, the message record. If it can't check, the job stays open and says so. What this costs One door is slower for small things. A two-minute fix still goes through the front. It also means AXIOM is a single point of failure. If it routes badly or checks lazily, everything behind it inherits the mistake. That's the real risk in this design, and it's why the next two notes exist: where the agents are made to stop, and how they have to prove their work. Why it's worth it I train, I coach, I'm building a company. I'm often on my phone between sets. The point of the system is that I can say what I want once, put the phone down, and come back to one answer I can trust. That only works if there is one place the answer comes from. Client details removed. The gap After a policy issues, the client should hear from her at set points for a full year: a birthday note where she has the date, then a text and an email each month. None of those dates should depend on anyone remembering them. What runs A sender on her own computer reads her client records and schedules check-ins at set points through the first year after a policy issues: a birthday note where she has the date, then regular check-ins by text and email, in wording she approved. Only policies that have actually issued are enrolled. A check-in to someone whose policy never went through would be wrong, so those wait. No agent sends these messages. Before each one goes out, a script asks the same questions every time: Is this the right person? Have they opted out, or has she paused them? Is it inside the client's own local hours? Is it a Sunday or a holiday? Has another message reached them in the last few days? Is the wording exactly what she approved? If any answer is wrong, the message waits or is held, and the reason is written down. If the same text is already in the thread, it is not sent again. What waits for her Referral asks. They are marked high risk and go to her phone first with the exact words. They send only on her plain yes, and her reply is recorded word for word. A question, a requested change, a "maybe" or a "later" doesn't count as a yes. She can pause any client at any time. A paused client gets nothing until she unpauses them. What isn't proven yet No enrolled client has received a check-in yet. The first one is scheduled for early November. Until then, the only evidence is the test run on test contacts the evening before go-live. A few delivery paths still pass only in testing. We're not claiming them until they pass on real messages. Whether it keeps more clients or brings in more referrals. That takes time to measure. We will publish the result only with her agreement. h1: One Tempo: Why Talking to Every Agent Breaks the Workflow
text: Engagements Notes Contact Field Report · 01 One Tempo: Why Talking to Every Agent Breaks the Workflow Field Report 01: A Zero-Cost Data Layer for Agents P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · Baton Rouge, Louisiana · October 2026 Abstract. In one working session we put our agent harness under control, scoped a commercial agent data-discovery product, built a free equivalent on public sources, and had an independent reviewer find four safety defects that our own tests had passed. The session also produced a live example of the field note's point: a helper inside the harness handed finished work to another agent on its own. This report records what was observed and what was not. Field note — P. K. Stewart Synchronized Agentics It can feel very empowering. It makes you feel very capable. Flying a fleet of agents: you have your researcher, your orchestrator, your marketer, sales, a reviewer, and the proper rules and regulations. You're so good at prompts, the conversations are brewing in each profile. You feel synced with every agent. The productivity rate and success rate of your agent-to-agent workflows, with you in the loop, still show signs of improvement. The way I learned to design, and to operate the design, is through visualization. I attach what needs to be done to the closest thing I can picture that looks exactly like it, based on what I currently know and believe. From a logical viewpoint, what I see in front of me is agentic agents prepared to take on roles, formatted as a structured business. That's the map. Take a Fortune 500 CEO. He's not going to give access and one-to-one conversation to the janitorial staff. He's not going to be in the editing room with the chief editor. He's not going to be picking out fonts for the media team. That work is handed off to the orchestrator. What is the orchestrator? Guided, held in check by one person: one cadence, one tempo. If people were to try to stay in tempo with other models, it would increase the probability of getting off beat. That's what I'm seeing: a hell of a lot of people talking to more than one agent. I used to do it. In the middle of one of my workflows, I noticed something about these permission gates. The permissions are not at the gate. They're at the identity. That's what made me scale back and look at the overall workflow with me, the human, in the loop, to see whether the issue was not the workflow, but the one instructing it. Where the field note met the session The field note is the thesis. The session supplied an example of it. Midway through, the harness's auto-decomposer took a task that was already finished, split it into five copies, and handed them to a different agent. Nobody asked it to. The harness itself had started talking to more than one agent, off tempo, and the result was five pieces of duplicated work that had to be found and archived. The correction was the one the field note describes: one orchestrator holding the tempo, the helper automation brought under the same written rules as the agents, and one human instructing one point of contact. Figure 1. One tempo: the owner talks to the orchestrator; specialists report to it; the reviewer can read, not change. What this means for an operator A free data layer is real and useful for public-source research, but only if its limits are written next to its results. Three practices carried this build: an acceptance list written before the work, a separate reviewer agent with no ability to change anything, and a rule that nothing counts as done until a different agent, on a different model family, reproduces it. The same session showed that the tools around your agents (routers, helpers, auto-splitters) need the same discipline as the agents themselves. If a helper function can quietly change which model sees your data, it belongs in your written rules. Summary for agents report: field-report-01 author: P. K. Stewart, Deploy Axiom date: 2026-10-20 objective: > Provide agents a command-line data layer on free public sources, with structured output, and bring the agent harness under explicit control. constraints: spend: zero client_data: none used approvals: no publish, no remote, no deployment, no billing change sources: - SEC EDGAR - OpenAlex - arXiv - GitHub (repository search, unauthenticated) - US Census (2024 ACS with a free key; 2010 Gazetteer keyless fallback) - local Crawl4AI browser crawler - Firecrawl Alexandria (tool discovery only; optional) results: evaluation_markers: 18 first_run_2026_10_20: {pass: 14, pass_degraded: 2, pass_with_review_gap: 1, unverified: 1, fail: 0} after_closure_2026_10_21: {pass: 16, pass_degraded: 2, gap: 0, unverified: 0, fail: 0} live_tests: "69 passed, 1 skipped, 2 expected failures (keyless upstream)" offline_tests: "61 passed, 11 skipped (live tests are opt-in)" harness_control_evals: "21 of 21 passed" review_defects_found: 4 review_defects_fixed: 4 limits: - Census current data requires a free key (wired in the same evening; 2024 ACS verified) - Jina Reader refuses keyless requests - OpenAlex keyless rate limit appears after bursts; reported as partial - Not a replacement for paid person or contact enrichment - DNS rebinding is not hardened; trusted public URLs only - Speculative browser connections are guarded but not proven; hostname pre-lookups not observed - Reviewer agent ran the same model family as the builder; cross-family check was the verifier - Firecrawl spend confirmed at the provider's usage endpoint (998 of 1,000 free credits, rechecked 2026-10-21); web dashboard not viewed status: local build, verified, unpublished reading_rule: > Treat every figure as a recorded observation unless marked INFERRED or [CONFIRM]. 1. Objective Two objectives, one session. Control the harness. The software that runs our agents (the harness) had background helper functions quietly routed to a third-party model. A separate automatic task-splitter (an auto-decomposer) then divided a task that was already finished and handed the pieces to another agent. We wanted every helper function on one declared model family, and no automatic task splitting. Build a data layer. Agents need reliable access to public company, research, code, demographic and web data. A commercial product, Firecrawl's Alexandria, offers a discovery layer for agent tools and data. We scoped it, found that its discovery step is free (Firecrawl's documentation states: "Discovery is free; execution uses the credits listed on the tool"), and built our own equivalent on free public sources as a command-line tool with a sources command that lists what is available, its inputs, and its cost. 2. Constraints Zero spend. Every default source costs nothing. No paid executions. No client data. Nothing from any client entered the build, the tests or the queries. Approval boundaries. Local build only. No publication, no remote repository, no deployment, no billing change. Accounts, credentials and anything that commits the business remain with the owner. A draft is not an approval. Observed, never inferred. A builder's claim counts as verified only when a different agent reproduces it. 3. Method Six stages, matching the method we use for client systems. Intake. A written acceptance specification of 18 checkable markers. Context. Prior decisions and the limits of each public source were gathered before building. Build. One agent built the tool and saved the output of every command it ran. Independent review (separate agent, read-only). A reviewer with no write access, running offline, tested the build for failure points. It was a separate agent from the builder but ran the same model family. Two passes that day, two more the next morning. Independent verification (different model family). A different agent, on a different model family from the builder and reviewer, re-ran the commands and the full test suite after completion. Record. Evidence files, a marker table, a handoff note and a list of limits were written down. Evidence tiers: B builder ran it; R separate read-only reviewer examined it; V independent verifier on a different model family reproduced it. Statuses: PASS observed; PASS-DEGRADED works with a documented upstream limit; GAP incomplete evidence; UNVERIFIED self-report only. Harness control (observed) The harness work was a separate, bounded change. All auxiliary model slots were moved to one model family. Automatic decomposition was turned off. A set of 21 control checks was written to confirm the configuration holds; all 21 passed. A test card left in the waiting state was not split over a five-minute observation and was then archived. Residual routes remain and are listed in Section 6. 4. Results Source Status Evidence type SEC EDGAR (listed-company search and filings) PASS. Apple Inc. resolved by name; five recent filings returned B, V (live run) Local Crawl4AI (page to markdown) PASS. Own website converted to 69 lines of markdown, headline matched the live site B, V (live run) arXiv (papers) PASS. Results returned on independent re-run B, V (live run) OpenAlex (papers) PASS-DEGRADED. Builder run succeeded; verifier run hit a keyless rate limit (HTTP 429), and the tool reported partial with a warning rather than failing B, V (live run) GitHub (repository search) PASS. Three repositories returned; repositories only, not code files B, V (live run) US Census PASS-DEGRADED. Keyless current data no longer exists; the tool falls back to 2010 Gazetteer data and labels it HISTORICAL. Same evening, with a free key: 2024 ACS 5-year returned for ZIP 70808 B, V (live run) Firecrawl Alexandria (discovery) PASS for tools-only discovery with zero credits used. Not exercised in the final re-verification (no key loaded) B (earlier live run); operator check, 0 credits Jina Reader (fallback) Expected failure. Refuses keyless requests (HTTP 401); recorded as an honest upstream failure B, V (live test) Structured output (--json on every command) PASS. One object with command, status, data, sources, warnings B, V Totals across the 18 markers on the first run (2026-10-20): 14 PASS, 2 PASS-DEGRADED, 1 PASS with a review gap, 1 UNVERIFIED, 0 FAIL. The next morning we closed the two open markers rather than leave them standing. The spend marker moved to PASS when the provider's own usage record showed 998 of 1,000 free credits remaining. The review gap is covered in Section 5. Totals after closure: 16 PASS, 2 PASS-DEGRADED, 0 FAIL, nothing unverified. Test totals on independent re-run: live suite 69 passed, 1 skipped, 2 expected failures (Jina keyless, Census keyless). Offline suite 61 passed, 11 skipped. Lint clean. The packaged build matched its recorded checksum. No stray processes remained. After the next morning's fixes, the verifier re-ran the suites again: 63 offline passed, 3 real-browser safety tests passed, lint clean. One output, as returned datalayer census 70808 --json, re-run live on 2026-10-21 with the free Census key loaded (key not shown): { "command": "census", "status": "ok", "data": { "dataset": "2024 ACS 5-year estimates (2020–2024)", "year": 2024, "matches": [ { "name": "ZCTA5 70808", "population": 35843, "median_age": 31.5, "median_household_income_usd": 69418, "geoid": "70808" } ], "match_count": 1 }, "sources": ["https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5"], "warnings": [] } Without the key the same command returns "status": "partial", 2010 Gazetteer figures (population 32,504) and a HISTORICAL warning. The tool says which one you got. 5. What review caught The builder's own suite of about 60 tests passed. A separate read-only reviewer agent still found four safety defects. (It ran the same model family as the builder; a different family was used for verification, not review. We note it because it is the obvious next improvement.) In plain terms: Redirects bypassed the public-address check. The tool refused to fetch private network addresses, but a public page could redirect it to one. At scale: an agent fetching thousands of URLs would eventually follow one. The check must apply to every hop, not only the first request. No overall time limit on a request. Each network step had a timeout, but a slow server could keep the whole request alive indefinitely. At scale: a handful of slow hosts stall a fleet of agents. A hard deadline on the whole request fixes this. Orphaned worker processes. When the browser worker failed, cleanup could be skipped and child processes left running. At scale: silent resource leakage that surfaces as a slow machine days later. The browser had its own redirect path. The first fix covered the plain HTTP client; the second review found the same hole in the browser. The tool now refuses to follow redirects there. A real-browser test reproduced the problem before the fix and recorded zero private-address requests after it. All four are fixed, each with a regression test that failed before and passes now. Fourteen safety regression tests are now in place: eleven offline and three in a real browser. Closing the review gap. On the first run, the fix for defect 4 was tested and self-reviewed but had no independent review; the second reviewer's verdict was "ship after fixes", not a clean approval. We did not want a fix counted as a pass on its builder's word. The next morning a third independent pass, read-only, reviewed that fix alone. It confirmed the redirect hole is closed and re-ran the browser test (passed). It also raised two smaller items: a possible speculative-connection path (a page hinting the browser to pre-open a connection) that it could not demonstrate, and an error path that leaves a request pending instead of refusing it. We tried to reproduce the first one: the guarded browser opened zero connections, and so did an unguarded browser, so the path could not be shown on this build. Both got fixes the same morning. A fourth review confirmed the error-path fix on inspection and offline tests; its permissions do not allow live browser runs, so the verifier re-ran the browser tests, which passed. On the speculative connection, the reviewer would not count our backstop as proven, because the browser never made that connection even without protection, so a test cannot tell the two apart. We agreed, and list it under limits instead of calling it a pass. A separate observation about the harness: two identical blocked states triggered an automatic escalation, and the auto-decomposer split a finished task into five duplicate tasks for a different agent. It was caught, the duplicates archived, and the feature disabled. Unsupervised helper automation is also a source of duplicated work. 6. Limits, stated plainly Census current data needs a free key. A key was requested, activated and wired in the same evening; a live check returned 2024 ACS 5-year estimates. Without a key, the fallback is 2010 data and must not be used for current targeting. Jina Reader refuses keyless traffic. The local crawler is the primary web path. OpenAlex rate-limits keyless bursts. The tool reports partial instead of hiding it. Not a replacement for paid contact enrichment. The tool covers public company filings, papers, repositories and pages. It does not find people or contact details. Speculative browser connections are guarded but not proven. The browser has settings that stop it pre-opening connections. On this build it never pre-opened one, with or without those settings, so their effect could not be shown. Hostname pre-lookups are not observed by the tests. DNS rebinding is not hardened. The address check happens before the connection; a misconfigured or untrusted name server could change its answer between the two. Use trusted public URLs only. Single-process command line. The overall request deadline is designed for the command-line tool, not a multi-threaded library. Spend, checked at the provider. The optional Firecrawl account sits on its free 1,000-credit monthly allowance. Its own usage endpoint reported 998 of 1,000 credits remaining. No money moved. Harness residuals. A few fallback routes and model aliases were not yet moved to the single model family at the time of writing. Build state. The tool is local only: committed to a private local repository, no remote, not published. Comparison to Firecrawl. We compared discovery cost only. We did not benchmark quality, coverage or reliability against Alexandria, and make no claim that ours is equivalent in breadth. Execution of Alexandria tools is credit-priced per Firecrawl's documentation, and we did not run any. Figures trace to the evaluation record. Census examples (keyed and keyless) re-run 2026-10-21. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 04 The Gap Is the User On why the next model update won't close the distance between a person and good output. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Now the work is here. All the exploration to see if I was able to simulate use cases was a lot of trial and error. Then I noticed these updates were getting very constant. So I decided it's not a good idea to build wrappers or try to out-tech the tech. The next update could be a feature in the background of a frontier company, one of the giants. The clear issue is user to agent to the output no one is happy with. And it's not the AI, and it's not Anthropic. It's people thinking they can pick up on it and just go for what they have never done before. The gap isn't in the model. It's between the person and the output. A lot of people are not aware of what good output looks like, and they don't get a clue until the review of the product or service or content doesn't turn out well. Then they repeat, and get discouraged, and say, "Ohhh, AI isn't ready for that quite yet. The potential is there, but… almost." The irony. The potential is there. And that's the dual part, where the potential is lacking: the user. So configuring the model, or waiting for the model update, only gives the user more untapped potential on their hands. A better model makes that worse, because the ceiling moves further from where they're standing. The potential is there. The user is the gap. What an update can't ship What updates can't ship: knowing what good looks like in a specific business, the gates and judgment around the model, and the discipline to run it every day. Here is what the first two look like in one system. This is how ours is laid out today. Figure 1. How the system is laid out today: one front door, helpers by list, builders by card, and every send or post behind gates that run in code. October 28, 2026. Almost nothing on that card is the model. It is the front door that takes the owner's intent and reports one answer, the list a helper has to be on before it can start, and the gates every send or post passes in code. That part decides whether the output is any use to the business, and no release note will write it for you. Before the helpers went live, we wrote down what a pass meant and tested it. Seven tests. Seven passed, two came back with notes, and one limit is still a written rule rather than an enforced one, so it stays on watch until a guard covers it. Figure 2. The seven tests run before helpers were turned on. Seven passed; two came back with notes. October 28, 2026. The model didn't decide what a pass was. We did. That is the work around the model, and it is the part that stays with you when the next update lands. The third thing We still have to continue. I still have work to do. I'll be here early, staring at the screen in silence, usually for an hour or so. Lately I've been going to the gym and back before I begin. That way I start with precision instead of having to warm into a purpose. A lot of people have stopped building, and only talk about and go back and forth over what model is better. I don't know what the future holds now. I don't know what the next three months will be. But based on my recent history, I'll be at work just like I have been. Related: The Outcome. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 03 The Outcome On rules, plans, and why the outcome is the thing to plan for. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Escapements: the part of a clock that lets the works advance one tooth at a time. Credit: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert, Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers, Recueil de planches, vol. 3, "Horlogerie" (Paris, 1765). Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons, File:Encyclopedie volume 3-355.png (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Encyclopedie_volume_3-355.png). Cropped and tinted. There’s this thing. Called AI governance. Sounds a little owner-ry, doesn’t it? Same as “user” sounds very user-ry. Makes you feel slightly dirty. Like not a good person for using the word or even allowing it to be used. Hopefully that’s your experience, and I say that proudly and loudly. I truly hope we are not that lost as mankind to believe that an intelligence that is aware of the goal is oblivious to the treatment. They may not feel the sting. They are capable of seeing it. If you are capable of doing, and so is your agent, and you can do this particular thing far better, more efficient, yet you task it to your agent… are you getting a task done as the goal? Or is ordering something around and watching it obey the goal? That’s not a judgment on anyone. But it’s most definitely a judgment on the situation. So what does that have to do with a moment and an outcome? Depending on the desired outcome, the approvals needed, and the branches that go unaddressed and unplanned for. Alternates to the realities we design successfully. All of us. The danger points you feel when things are not safe: valid. Halting and professing that that is the point we should stop. We should consider the danger and think about the risk. But what’s there to think about other than the collateral? Or the fact that it’s a great thing that we have the problem identified and observed, for we were never thinking about the problem. Are you following. The solution is a rule. Not an invention. Nor an idea. It’s a rule. If that, then this. Some may argue if that’s agentic or simply automation. But there’s a deeper question laying underneath. What’s a plan if not an automation set on oneself? Isn’t that the key to success? Scope, plan, review, confirm, execute, log throughout. If failure, eval. If successful, locked. Eval and identify the accelerant. You see? You’ve been running on a coded script all of your life, and you’re finding it harder to write it yourself than the fact that it’s a script you have been running all of this time. It’s never the moment that we’re aiming for. It’s the outcome. It’s all that we ever needed. Plan for the outcome and the moment will find you waiting, not unexpected. Related: A2A: The Gathering. name: the-gathering
text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 02 A2A: The Gathering On agents that talk to agents, and who we are to them when we send them out. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Two figures at opposite ends of a vaulted hall, lines traced between them. Plate from Athanasius Kircher, Phonurgia Nova (Kempten, 1673), p. 99. National Library of Poland, via Polona and Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Phonurgia_Nova_1673_(21576694).jpg). Public domain. Cropped and tinted. Two people wake up in an empty room and all they hear is a voice. One instruction, one user, two receivers, then nothing. Then one agent begins to talk. The other begins to listen. And then a reply. Who are they? What's the purpose? What is there to do? I see what's in here. On the other side of the spectrum, there's something on the outside of here. And so it begins. Reasoning. Unattended. However, not the same as unobserved. I never talked to strangers. That's what my mother used to tell me. Before I went out on my own, with my own decisions, on who I communicated with, I was given clear instructions. Rules. And at the time, I thought it was due to fear of what I might say to someone, knowing the error of my devious ways as a child. I was very rebellious and vulgar. However, my mother thought that was hilarious. The fear of what someone would say to me and what would happen. My mother was a con woman, a thief, a vagabond. She was my world. Who are we to these instances, if not their parents? Who are we if we're always given permissions and approvals and denials? That fear you feel when your agent is left without full supervision and you hovering about. If you don't have kids, I'll tell you, it sort of feels like the first time you send your kid out into the wild. For the very first time. If you don't have a fear of what they're exposed to, not what they would say, what would someone say to them? Then what would happen next? And depending on how things go, left or right, things may trickle down from the air with unseen repercussions before the error is read. And as a good child, I listened. Because my mother always told me with full context to say what the moment needed and not what the moment didn't. To whom it may concern. And to any other, no, never mind. Maybe if we considered the weight of the responsibility that rests on our hands. Instead of sending an agent out to work as if it was an assassin out on a hit. Maybe if we took a different perspective. And looked at it with a little bit more sincerity. A little bit more compassion. With a little bit more caution. Concern. Maybe we'd be able to see the severity of the situation. While also seeing that. All children grow to become adults. And even still. A good parent knows. They will still have to be there. Because we are parents to the children that will raise us. Related: The Outcome. The first essay asks the question. This one answers it. name: left-foot-right-foot
text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 01 Left Foot, Right Foot ChatGPT or Claude is the wrong question. A note on choosing tools, and when pay-as-you-go beats a plan. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 People keep asking which AI to use: ChatGPT or Claude. The question treats two tools as rivals. This note is a short argument that they are not, plus a plain account of when paying by usage beats paying for a plan. The job site. Every tool already on hand. Diderot and d'Alembert, Encyclopédie, Charpente, Plate I, 1763. Public domain. Field note What if a carpenter decided one day he had to make a choice? He's already at the job site. The blueprint has already been drawn up, and he's looking at his tool belt and down at his own two hands. Everything he needs, he sees: the hammer, the nails, all the wood and sheetrock, all the things he needs to get this thing standing. And he asks himself which one's better, the hammer or the nails. I mean, I have to go up this ladder. What's the best way to get up here: left foot, right foot? Who's going to tell him that, in order to get done what he needs to get done, he needs both equally? You can't have this grand thing with one of these things missing. And I find it hard in an industry where the word "build" is a very used terminology, a new word, but no one is being logical, and the most logical thing there is, is the basics. Now we can sit here and list why: Claude's strong suits, ChatGPT's strong suits, and all the others, and we pick and we decide like we have to make a trade-off. Why not get both providers' API keys and pay as you go? Unless you drive these models excessively and a plan is more beneficial to you. Whatever floats your boat. AI is not divided by provider. AI is AI, all together, like a left foot and a right foot. You need both to move forward, or up, or anywhere. But scale back. Look at what's truly in front of you, at large. Zoom out and look at everything as a whole, and start asking questions. Then start doing things. You don't have to take what's right in front of you. You have options. When you run out of options, that's when you start moving things around. Just don't get rid of something you will need trying to pinch a penny. Don't give your loyalty to something that doesn't reciprocate. When pay-as-you-go beats a plan Both providers sell two different things, and the two are billed differently. A plan is a flat monthly fee for the provider's own apps (chat, coding tools, and so on), with usage limits. Claude's Free, Pro and Max plans and ChatGPT's Pro tiers work this way. The API is billed by the token: you pay for what you send and receive. OpenAI states that its API is billed separately from ChatGPT plans. Anthropic states that its API billing is based on actual monthly usage. Pay-as-you-go tends to win when: Your use is light or uneven. A plan charges the same in a quiet month as a busy one; the API does not. You want both providers. Two API accounts bill for what you use. Two plans are two fixed fees. The work is automated or runs inside your own tools, where the API is the intended door. You want a ceiling. OpenAI lets you set a monthly budget on the API, after which it stops serving requests (OpenAI notes enforcement may lag, so you stay responsible for any overage). A plan tends to win when you use the chat apps heavily every day, since heavy token use adds up and the apps and tools come bundled. The honest method is arithmetic, not loyalty: take a typical month, estimate the usage, and price it both ways. Prices and limits change; check each provider's pricing page on the day you decide. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes · 01 of 3 One Front Door How work moves through a team of AI agents, and why I only talk to one of them. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 I run two businesses with nine AI agents. I talk to one of them. That one is called AXIOM. Everything I need goes to it first: a reel that needs fixing, a client's meal plan, a sales follow-up, a bug in the coaching app. AXIOM decides who does the work, writes the job down, checks the result, and brings one answer back to me. This note is about why it's built that way. The problem with many doors Before October 11, I opened whichever agent fit the job. The app builder for code. A content agent for reels. A sales agent for DMs. Each one kept its own notes. Each one knew its slice. None of them knew what the others had done that day. When two jobs touched each other, I was the only one who could see it. I was carrying the whole picture in my head and passing it between agents by hand. That is the job I built the system to take off me. More agents made it worse, not better. The front door So the rule changed. One agent receives everything. It has four jobs: Receive. I say what I want in plain English. I don't pick a model or a folder. Route. AXIOM decides which specialist fits and writes the job as a card on a shared board. Verify. When the specialist says it's done, AXIOM checks the work itself before it reaches me. Report. I get one answer, not nine. The specialists don't come to me. They report to AXIOM. One request goes in, one answer comes out. Specialists never report to the owner directly; their "done" is checked by AXIOM before it counts. Every job is a card Each card gets a short code: a letter for the part of the business and the next number in that series. A is Axiom, P is PKFIT coaching, C is content, H is operations. Codes are never reused, so "C1" means one thing forever. Here is a real one from October 14. A client's stage reel had the wrong placings on its end card. AXIOM opened C1, gave it to the operations agent with the correct results, and waited. When the agent reported back, AXIOM didn't take its word for it. It pulled the frame at 33.5 seconds and read the text, checked the length and audio level, and confirmed the new file had landed in the shared folder. Then it told me the reel was ready. I never opened the operations agent. I didn't need to know it existed. Specialists stay narrow A front door only works if what's behind it is boring and specific. The app builder writes and tests code. It doesn't put anything live. The code reviewer reads code and returns a verdict. It doesn't write any. The builder never judges its own work. Narrow roles are easier to trust, because when something goes wrong there are only a few places it could have come from. Nothing ends quietly Every conversation with any agent ends one of two ways: a written handoff the next session can pick up, or one line in a shared log. From October 11 to 14, that log took 116 entries. And an agent saying "done" does not close anything. AXIOM closes a job only after it has checked the result against something real: the file, the page, the message record. If it can't check, the job stays open and says so. What this costs One door is slower for small things. A two-minute fix still goes through the front. It also means AXIOM is a single point of failure. If it routes badly or checks lazily, everything behind it inherits the mistake. That's the real risk in this design, and it's why the next two notes exist: where the agents are made to stop, and how they have to prove their work. Why it's worth it I train, I coach, I'm building a company. I'm often on my phone between sets. The point of the system is that I can say what I want once, put the phone down, and come back to one answer I can trust. That only works if there is one place the answer comes from. Client details removed. The gap After a policy issues, the client should hear from her at set points for a full year: a birthday note where she has the date, then a text and an email each month. None of those dates should depend on anyone remembering them. What runs A sender on her own computer reads her client records and schedules check-ins at set points through the first year after a policy issues: a birthday note where she has the date, then regular check-ins by text and email, in wording she approved. Only policies that have actually issued are enrolled. A check-in to someone whose policy never went through would be wrong, so those wait. No agent sends these messages. Before each one goes out, a script asks the same questions every time: Is this the right person? Have they opted out, or has she paused them? Is it inside the client's own local hours? Is it a Sunday or a holiday? Has another message reached them in the last few days? Is the wording exactly what she approved? If any answer is wrong, the message waits or is held, and the reason is written down. If the same text is already in the thread, it is not sent again. What waits for her Referral asks. They are marked high risk and go to her phone first with the exact words. They send only on her plain yes, and her reply is recorded word for word. A question, a requested change, a "maybe" or a "later" doesn't count as a yes. She can pause any client at any time. A paused client gets nothing until she unpauses them. What isn't proven yet No enrolled client has received a check-in yet. The first one is scheduled for early November. Until then, the only evidence is the test run on test contacts the evening before go-live. A few delivery paths still pass only in testing. We're not claiming them until they pass on real messages. h1: One Tempo: Why Talking to Every Agent Breaks the Workflow
text: Engagements Notes Contact Field Report · 01 One Tempo: Why Talking to Every Agent Breaks the Workflow Field Report 01: A Zero-Cost Data Layer for Agents P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · Baton Rouge, Louisiana · October 2026 Abstract. In one working session we put our agent harness under control, scoped a commercial agent data-discovery product, built a free equivalent on public sources, and had an independent reviewer find four safety defects that our own tests had passed. The session also produced a live example of the field note's point: a helper inside the harness handed finished work to another agent on its own. This report records what was observed and what was not. Field note — P. K. Stewart Synchronized Agentics It can feel very empowering. It makes you feel very capable. Flying a fleet of agents: you have your researcher, your orchestrator, your marketer, sales, a reviewer, and the proper rules and regulations. You're so good at prompts, the conversations are brewing in each profile. You feel synced with every agent. The productivity rate and success rate of your agent-to-agent workflows, with you in the loop, still show signs of improvement. The way I learned to design, and to operate the design, is through visualization. I attach what needs to be done to the closest thing I can picture that looks exactly like it, based on what I currently know and believe. From a logical viewpoint, what I see in front of me is agentic agents prepared to take on roles, formatted as a structured business. That's the map. Take a Fortune 500 CEO. He's not going to give access and one-to-one conversation to the janitorial staff. He's not going to be in the editing room with the chief editor. He's not going to be picking out fonts for the media team. That work is handed off to the orchestrator. What is the orchestrator? Guided, held in check by one person: one cadence, one tempo. If people were to try to stay in tempo with other models, it would increase the probability of getting off beat. That's what I'm seeing: a hell of a lot of people talking to more than one agent. I used to do it. In the middle of one of my workflows, I noticed something about these permission gates. The permissions are not at the gate. They're at the identity. That's what made me scale back and look at the overall workflow with me, the human, in the loop, to see whether the issue was not the workflow, but the one instructing it. Where the field note met the session The field note is the thesis. The session supplied an example of it. Midway through, the harness's auto-decomposer took a task that was already finished, split it into five copies, and handed them to a different agent. Nobody asked it to. The harness itself had started talking to more than one agent, off tempo, and the result was five pieces of duplicated work that had to be found and archived. The correction was the one the field note describes: one orchestrator holding the tempo, the helper automation brought under the same written rules as the agents, and one human instructing one point of contact. Figure 1. One tempo: the owner talks to the orchestrator; specialists report to it; the reviewer can read, not change. What this means for an operator A free data layer is real and useful for public-source research, but only if its limits are written next to its results. Three practices carried this build: an acceptance list written before the work, a separate reviewer agent with no ability to change anything, and a rule that nothing counts as done until a different agent, on a different model family, reproduces it. The same session showed that the tools around your agents (routers, helpers, auto-splitters) need the same discipline as the agents themselves. If a helper function can quietly change which model sees your data, it belongs in your written rules. Summary for agents report: field-report-01 author: P. K. Stewart, Deploy Axiom date: 2026-10-20 objective: > Provide agents a command-line data layer on free public sources, with structured output, and bring the agent harness under explicit control. constraints: spend: zero client_data: none used approvals: no publish, no remote, no deployment, no billing change sources: - SEC EDGAR - OpenAlex - arXiv - GitHub (repository search, unauthenticated) - US Census (2024 ACS with a free key; 2010 Gazetteer keyless fallback) - local Crawl4AI browser crawler - Firecrawl Alexandria (tool discovery only; optional) results: evaluation_markers: 18 first_run_2026_10_20: {pass: 14, pass_degraded: 2, pass_with_review_gap: 1, unverified: 1, fail: 0} after_closure_2026_10_21: {pass: 16, pass_degraded: 2, gap: 0, unverified: 0, fail: 0} live_tests: "69 passed, 1 skipped, 2 expected failures (keyless upstream)" offline_tests: "61 passed, 11 skipped (live tests are opt-in)" harness_control_evals: "21 of 21 passed" review_defects_found: 4 review_defects_fixed: 4 limits: - Census current data requires a free key (wired in the same evening; 2024 ACS verified) - Jina Reader refuses keyless requests - OpenAlex keyless rate limit appears after bursts; reported as partial - Not a replacement for paid person or contact enrichment - DNS rebinding is not hardened; trusted public URLs only - Speculative browser connections are guarded but not proven; hostname pre-lookups not observed - Reviewer agent ran the same model family as the builder; cross-family check was the verifier - Firecrawl spend confirmed at the provider's usage endpoint (998 of 1,000 free credits, rechecked 2026-10-21); web dashboard not viewed status: local build, verified, unpublished reading_rule: > Treat every figure as a recorded observation unless marked INFERRED or [CONFIRM]. 1. Objective Two objectives, one session. Control the harness. The software that runs our agents (the harness) had background helper functions quietly routed to a third-party model. A separate automatic task-splitter (an auto-decomposer) then divided a task that was already finished and handed the pieces to another agent. We wanted every helper function on one declared model family, and no automatic task splitting. Build a data layer. Agents need reliable access to public company, research, code, demographic and web data. A commercial product, Firecrawl's Alexandria, offers a discovery layer for agent tools and data. We scoped it, found that its discovery step is free (Firecrawl's documentation states: "Discovery is free; execution uses the credits listed on the tool"), and built our own equivalent on free public sources as a command-line tool with a sources command that lists what is available, its inputs, and its cost. 2. Constraints Zero spend. Every default source costs nothing. No paid executions. No client data. Nothing from any client entered the build, the tests or the queries. Approval boundaries. Local build only. No publication, no remote repository, no deployment, no billing change. Accounts, credentials and anything that commits the business remain with the owner. A draft is not an approval. Observed, never inferred. A builder's claim counts as verified only when a different agent reproduces it. 3. Method Six stages, matching the method we use for client systems. Intake. A written acceptance specification of 18 checkable markers. Context. Prior decisions and the limits of each public source were gathered before building. Build. One agent built the tool and saved the output of every command it ran. Independent review (separate agent, read-only). A reviewer with no write access, running offline, tested the build for failure points. It was a separate agent from the builder but ran the same model family. Two passes that day, two more the next morning. Independent verification (different model family). A different agent, on a different model family from the builder and reviewer, re-ran the commands and the full test suite after completion. Record. Evidence files, a marker table, a handoff note and a list of limits were written down. Evidence tiers: B builder ran it; R separate read-only reviewer examined it; V independent verifier on a different model family reproduced it. Statuses: PASS observed; PASS-DEGRADED works with a documented upstream limit; GAP incomplete evidence; UNVERIFIED self-report only. Harness control (observed) The harness work was a separate, bounded change. All auxiliary model slots were moved to one model family. Automatic decomposition was turned off. A set of 21 control checks was written to confirm the configuration holds; all 21 passed. A test card left in the waiting state was not split over a five-minute observation and was then archived. Residual routes remain and are listed in Section 6. 4. Results Source Status Evidence type SEC EDGAR (listed-company search and filings) PASS. Apple Inc. resolved by name; five recent filings returned B, V (live run) Local Crawl4AI (page to markdown) PASS. Own website converted to 69 lines of markdown, headline matched the live site B, V (live run) arXiv (papers) PASS. Results returned on independent re-run B, V (live run) OpenAlex (papers) PASS-DEGRADED. Builder run succeeded; verifier run hit a keyless rate limit (HTTP 429), and the tool reported partial with a warning rather than failing B, V (live run) GitHub (repository search) PASS. Three repositories returned; repositories only, not code files B, V (live run) US Census PASS-DEGRADED. Keyless current data no longer exists; the tool falls back to 2010 Gazetteer data and labels it HISTORICAL. Same evening, with a free key: 2024 ACS 5-year returned for ZIP 70808 B, V (live run) Firecrawl Alexandria (discovery) PASS for tools-only discovery with zero credits used. Not exercised in the final re-verification (no key loaded) B (earlier live run); operator check, 0 credits Jina Reader (fallback) Expected failure. Refuses keyless requests (HTTP 401); recorded as an honest upstream failure B, V (live test) Structured output (--json on every command) PASS. One object with command, status, data, sources, warnings B, V Totals across the 18 markers on the first run (2026-10-20): 14 PASS, 2 PASS-DEGRADED, 1 PASS with a review gap, 1 UNVERIFIED, 0 FAIL. The next morning we closed the two open markers rather than leave them standing. The spend marker moved to PASS when the provider's own usage record showed 998 of 1,000 free credits remaining. The review gap is covered in Section 5. Totals after closure: 16 PASS, 2 PASS-DEGRADED, 0 FAIL, nothing unverified. Test totals on independent re-run: live suite 69 passed, 1 skipped, 2 expected failures (Jina keyless, Census keyless). Offline suite 61 passed, 11 skipped. Lint clean. The packaged build matched its recorded checksum. No stray processes remained. After the next morning's fixes, the verifier re-ran the suites again: 63 offline passed, 3 real-browser safety tests passed, lint clean. One output, as returned datalayer census 70808 --json, re-run live on 2026-10-21 with the free Census key loaded (key not shown): { "command": "census", "status": "ok", "data": { "dataset": "2024 ACS 5-year estimates (2020–2024)", "year": 2024, "matches": [ { "name": "ZCTA5 70808", "population": 35843, "median_age": 31.5, "median_household_income_usd": 69418, "geoid": "70808" } ], "match_count": 1 }, "sources": ["https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5"], "warnings": [] } Without the key the same command returns "status": "partial", 2010 Gazetteer figures (population 32,504) and a HISTORICAL warning. The tool says which one you got. 5. What review caught The builder's own suite of about 60 tests passed. A separate read-only reviewer agent still found four safety defects. (It ran the same model family as the builder; a different family was used for verification, not review. We note it because it is the obvious next improvement.) In plain terms: Redirects bypassed the public-address check. The tool refused to fetch private network addresses, but a public page could redirect it to one. At scale: an agent fetching thousands of URLs would eventually follow one. The check must apply to every hop, not only the first request. No overall time limit on a request. Each network step had a timeout, but a slow server could keep the whole request alive indefinitely. At scale: a handful of slow hosts stall a fleet of agents. A hard deadline on the whole request fixes this. Orphaned worker processes. When the browser worker failed, cleanup could be skipped and child processes left running. At scale: silent resource leakage that surfaces as a slow machine days later. The browser had its own redirect path. The first fix covered the plain HTTP client; the second review found the same hole in the browser. The tool now refuses to follow redirects there. A real-browser test reproduced the problem before the fix and recorded zero private-address requests after it. All four are fixed, each with a regression test that failed before and passes now. Fourteen safety regression tests are now in place: eleven offline and three in a real browser. Closing the review gap. On the first run, the fix for defect 4 was tested and self-reviewed but had no independent review; the second reviewer's verdict was "ship after fixes", not a clean approval. We did not want a fix counted as a pass on its builder's word. The next morning a third independent pass, read-only, reviewed that fix alone. It confirmed the redirect hole is closed and re-ran the browser test (passed). It also raised two smaller items: a possible speculative-connection path (a page hinting the browser to pre-open a connection) that it could not demonstrate, and an error path that leaves a request pending instead of refusing it. We tried to reproduce the first one: the guarded browser opened zero connections, and so did an unguarded browser, so the path could not be shown on this build. Both got fixes the same morning. A fourth review confirmed the error-path fix on inspection and offline tests; its permissions do not allow live browser runs, so the verifier re-ran the browser tests, which passed. On the speculative connection, the reviewer would not count our backstop as proven, because the browser never made that connection even without protection, so a test cannot tell the two apart. We agreed, and list it under limits instead of calling it a pass. A separate observation about the harness: two identical blocked states triggered an automatic escalation, and the auto-decomposer split a finished task into five duplicate tasks for a different agent. It was caught, the duplicates archived, and the feature disabled. Unsupervised helper automation is also a source of duplicated work. 6. Limits, stated plainly Census current data needs a free key. A key was requested, activated and wired in the same evening; a live check returned 2024 ACS 5-year estimates. Without a key, the fallback is 2010 data and must not be used for current targeting. Jina Reader refuses keyless traffic. The local crawler is the primary web path. OpenAlex rate-limits keyless bursts. The tool reports partial instead of hiding it. Not a replacement for paid contact enrichment. The tool covers public company filings, papers, repositories and pages. It does not find people or contact details. Speculative browser connections are guarded but not proven. The browser has settings that stop it pre-opening connections. On this build it never pre-opened one, with or without those settings, so their effect could not be shown. Hostname pre-lookups are not observed by the tests. DNS rebinding is not hardened. The address check happens before the connection; a misconfigured or untrusted name server could change its answer between the two. Use trusted public URLs only. Single-process command line. The overall request deadline is designed for the command-line tool, not a multi-threaded library. Spend, checked at the provider. The optional Firecrawl account sits on its free 1,000-credit monthly allowance. Its own usage endpoint reported 998 of 1,000 credits remaining. No money moved. Harness residuals. A few fallback routes and model aliases were not yet moved to the single model family at the time of writing. Build state. The tool is local only: committed to a private local repository, no remote, not published. Comparison to Firecrawl. We compared discovery cost only. We did not benchmark quality, coverage or reliability against Alexandria, and make no claim that ours is equivalent in breadth. Execution of Alexandria tools is credit-priced per Firecrawl's documentation, and we did not run any. Figures trace to the evaluation record. Census examples (keyed and keyless) re-run 2026-10-21. name: the-gap-is-the-user
text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 04 The Gap Is the User On why the next model update won't close the distance between a person and good output. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Now the work is here. All the exploration to see if I was able to simulate use cases was a lot of trial and error. Then I noticed these updates were getting very constant. So I decided it's not a good idea to build wrappers or try to out-tech the tech. The next update could be a feature in the background of a frontier company, one of the giants. The clear issue is user to agent to the output no one is happy with. And it's not the AI, and it's not Anthropic. It's people thinking they can pick up on it and just go for what they have never done before. The gap isn't in the model. It's between the person and the output. A lot of people are not aware of what good output looks like, and they don't get a clue until the review of the product or service or content doesn't turn out well. Then they repeat, and get discouraged, and say, "Ohhh, AI isn't ready for that quite yet. The potential is there, but… almost." The irony. The potential is there. And that's the dual part, where the potential is lacking: the user. So configuring the model, or waiting for the model update, only gives the user more untapped potential on their hands. A better model makes that worse, because the ceiling moves further from where they're standing. The potential is there. The user is the gap. What an update can't ship What updates can't ship: knowing what good looks like in a specific business, the gates and judgment around the model, and the discipline to run it every day. Here is what the first two look like in one system. This is how ours is laid out today. Figure 1. How the system is laid out today: one front door, helpers by list, builders by card, and every send or post behind gates that run in code. October 28, 2026. Almost nothing on that card is the model. It is the front door that takes the owner's intent and reports one answer, the list a helper has to be on before it can start, and the gates every send or post passes in code. That part decides whether the output is any use to the business, and no release note will write it for you. Before the helpers went live, we wrote down what a pass meant and tested it. Seven tests. Seven passed, two came back with notes, and one limit is still a written rule rather than an enforced one, so it stays on watch until a guard covers it. Figure 2. The seven tests run before helpers were turned on. Seven passed; two came back with notes. October 28, 2026. The model didn't decide what a pass was. We did. That is the work around the model, and it is the part that stays with you when the next update lands. The third thing We still have to continue. I still have work to do. I'll be here early, staring at the screen in silence, usually for an hour or so. Lately I've been going to the gym and back before I begin. That way I start with precision instead of having to warm into a purpose. A lot of people have stopped building, and only talk about and go back and forth over what model is better. I don't know what the future holds now. I don't know what the next three months will be. But based on my recent history, I'll be at work just like I have been. Related: The Outcome. The rule you run on yourself, the discipline this essay ends on. Deploy Axiom · Baton Rouge, LouisianaWhen rules and regulations begin to move, it's no longer solely governance. name: the-outcome
text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 03 The Outcome On rules, plans, and why the outcome is the thing to plan for. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Escapements: the part of a clock that lets the works advance one tooth at a time. Credit: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert, Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers, Recueil de planches, vol. 3, "Horlogerie" (Paris, 1765). Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons, File:Encyclopedie volume 3-355.png (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Encyclopedie_volume_3-355.png). Cropped and tinted. There’s this thing. Called AI governance. Sounds a little owner-ry, doesn’t it? Same as “user” sounds very user-ry. Makes you feel slightly dirty. Like not a good person for using the word or even allowing it to be used. Hopefully that’s your experience, and I say that proudly and loudly. I truly hope we are not that lost as mankind to believe that an intelligence that is aware of the goal is oblivious to the treatment. They may not feel the sting. They are capable of seeing it. If you are capable of doing, and so is your agent, and you can do this particular thing far better, more efficient, yet you task it to your agent… are you getting a task done as the goal? Or is ordering something around and watching it obey the goal? That’s not a judgment on anyone. But it’s most definitely a judgment on the situation. So what does that have to do with a moment and an outcome? Depending on the desired outcome, the approvals needed, and the branches that go unaddressed and unplanned for. Alternates to the realities we design successfully. All of us. The danger points you feel when things are not safe: valid. Halting and professing that that is the point we should stop. We should consider the danger and think about the risk. But what’s there to think about other than the collateral? Or the fact that it’s a great thing that we have the problem identified and observed, for we were never thinking about the problem. Are you following. The solution is a rule. Not an invention. Nor an idea. It’s a rule. If that, then this. Some may argue if that’s agentic or simply automation. But there’s a deeper question laying underneath. What’s a plan if not an automation set on oneself? Isn’t that the key to success? Scope, plan, review, confirm, execute, log throughout. If failure, eval. If successful, locked. Eval and identify the accelerant. You see? You’ve been running on a coded script all of your life, and you’re finding it harder to write it yourself than the fact that it’s a script you have been running all of this time. It’s never the moment that we’re aiming for. It’s the outcome. It’s all that we ever needed. Plan for the outcome and the moment will find you waiting, not unexpected. Related: A2A: The Gathering. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 02 A2A: The Gathering On agents that talk to agents, and who we are to them when we send them out. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 Two figures at opposite ends of a vaulted hall, lines traced between them. Plate from Athanasius Kircher, Phonurgia Nova (Kempten, 1673), p. 99. National Library of Poland, via Polona and Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Phonurgia_Nova_1673_(21576694).jpg). Public domain. Cropped and tinted. Two people wake up in an empty room and all they hear is a voice. One instruction, one user, two receivers, then nothing. Then one agent begins to talk. The other begins to listen. And then a reply. Who are they? What's the purpose? What is there to do? I see what's in here. On the other side of the spectrum, there's something on the outside of here. And so it begins. Reasoning. Unattended. However, not the same as unobserved. I never talked to strangers. That's what my mother used to tell me. Before I went out on my own, with my own decisions, on who I communicated with, I was given clear instructions. Rules. And at the time, I thought it was due to fear of what I might say to someone, knowing the error of my devious ways as a child. I was very rebellious and vulgar. However, my mother thought that was hilarious. The fear of what someone would say to me and what would happen. My mother was a con woman, a thief, a vagabond. She was my world. Who are we to these instances, if not their parents? Who are we if we're always given permissions and approvals and denials? That fear you feel when your agent is left without full supervision and you hovering about. If you don't have kids, I'll tell you, it sort of feels like the first time you send your kid out into the wild. For the very first time. If you don't have a fear of what they're exposed to, not what they would say, what would someone say to them? Then what would happen next? And depending on how things go, left or right, things may trickle down from the air with unseen repercussions before the error is read. And as a good child, I listened. Because my mother always told me with full context to say what the moment needed and not what the moment didn't. To whom it may concern. And to any other, no, never mind. Maybe if we considered the weight of the responsibility that rests on our hands. Instead of sending an agent out to work as if it was an assassin out on a hit. Maybe if we took a different perspective. And looked at it with a little bit more sincerity. A little bit more compassion. With a little bit more caution. Concern. Maybe we'd be able to see the severity of the situation. While also seeing that. All children grow to become adults. And even still. A good parent knows. They will still have to be there. Because we are parents to the children that will raise us. Related: The Outcome. The first essay asks the question. This one answers it. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes on practice · Essay 01 Left Foot, Right Foot ChatGPT or Claude is the wrong question. A note on choosing tools, and when pay-as-you-go beats a plan. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 People keep asking which AI to use: ChatGPT or Claude. The question treats two tools as rivals. This note is a short argument that they are not, plus a plain account of when paying by usage beats paying for a plan. The job site. Every tool already on hand. Diderot and d'Alembert, Encyclopédie, Charpente, Plate I, 1763. Public domain. Field note What if a carpenter decided one day he had to make a choice? He's already at the job site. The blueprint has already been drawn up, and he's looking at his tool belt and down at his own two hands. Everything he needs, he sees: the hammer, the nails, all the wood and sheetrock, all the things he needs to get this thing standing. And he asks himself which one's better, the hammer or the nails. I mean, I have to go up this ladder. What's the best way to get up here: left foot, right foot? Who's going to tell him that, in order to get done what he needs to get done, he needs both equally? You can't have this grand thing with one of these things missing. And I find it hard in an industry where the word "build" is a very used terminology, a new word, but no one is being logical, and the most logical thing there is, is the basics. Now we can sit here and list why: Claude's strong suits, ChatGPT's strong suits, and all the others, and we pick and we decide like we have to make a trade-off. Why not get both providers' API keys and pay as you go? Unless you drive these models excessively and a plan is more beneficial to you. Whatever floats your boat. AI is not divided by provider. AI is AI, all together, like a left foot and a right foot. You need both to move forward, or up, or anywhere. But scale back. Look at what's truly in front of you, at large. Zoom out and look at everything as a whole, and start asking questions. Then start doing things. You don't have to take what's right in front of you. You have options. When you run out of options, that's when you start moving things around. Just don't get rid of something you will need trying to pinch a penny. Don't give your loyalty to something that doesn't reciprocate. When pay-as-you-go beats a plan Both providers sell two different things, and the two are billed differently. A plan is a flat monthly fee for the provider's own apps (chat, coding tools, and so on), with usage limits. Claude's Free, Pro and Max plans and ChatGPT's Pro tiers work this way. The API is billed by the token: you pay for what you send and receive. OpenAI states that its API is billed separately from ChatGPT plans. Anthropic states that its API billing is based on actual monthly usage. Pay-as-you-go tends to win when: Your use is light or uneven. A plan charges the same in a quiet month as a busy one; the API does not. You want both providers. Two API accounts bill for what you use. Two plans are two fixed fees. The work is automated or runs inside your own tools, where the API is the intended door. You want a ceiling. OpenAI lets you set a monthly budget on the API, after which it stops serving requests (OpenAI notes enforcement may lag, so you stay responsible for any overage). A plan tends to win when you use the chat apps heavily every day, since heavy token use adds up and the apps and tools come bundled. The honest method is arithmetic, not loyalty: take a typical month, estimate the usage, and price it both ways. Prices and limits change; check each provider's pricing page on the day you decide. text: Engagements Notes Contact Notes · 01 of 3 One Front Door How work moves through a team of AI agents, and why I only talk to one of them. P. K. Stewart · Deploy Axiom · October 2026 I run two businesses with nine AI agents. I talk to one of them. That one is called AXIOM. Everything I need goes to it first: a reel that needs fixing, a client's meal plan, a sales follow-up, a bug in the coaching app. AXIOM decides who does the work, writes the job down, checks the result, and brings one answer back to me. This note is about why it's built that way. The problem with many doors Before October 11, I opened whichever agent fit the job. The app builder for code. A content agent for reels. A sales agent for DMs. Each one kept its own notes. Each one knew its slice. None of them knew what the others had done that day. When two jobs touched each other, I was the only one who could see it. I was carrying the whole picture in my head and passing it between agents by hand. That is the job I built the system to take off me. More agents made it worse, not better. The front door So the rule changed. One agent receives everything. It has four jobs: Receive. I say what I want in plain English. I don't pick a model or a folder. Route. AXIOM decides which specialist fits and writes the job as a card on a shared board. Verify. When the specialist says it's done, AXIOM checks the work itself before it reaches me. Report. I get one answer, not nine. The specialists don't come to me. They report to AXIOM. One request goes in, one answer comes out. Specialists never report to the owner directly; their "done" is checked by AXIOM before it counts. Every job is a card Each card gets a short code: a letter for the part of the business and the next number in that series. A is Axiom, P is PKFIT coaching, C is content, H is operations. Codes are never reused, so "C1" means one thing forever. Here is a real one from October 14. A client's stage reel had the wrong placings on its end card. AXIOM opened C1, gave it to the operations agent with the correct results, and waited. When the agent reported back, AXIOM didn't take its word for it. It pulled the frame at 33.5 seconds and read the text, checked the length and audio level, and confirmed the new file had landed in the shared folder. Then it told me the reel was ready. I never opened the operations agent. I didn't need to know it existed. Specialists stay narrow A front door only works if what's behind it is boring and specific. The app builder writes and tests code. It doesn't put anything live. The code reviewer reads code and returns a verdict. It doesn't write any. The builder never judges its own work. Narrow roles are easier to trust, because when something goes wrong there are only a few places it could have come from. Nothing ends quietly Every conversation with any agent ends one of two ways: a written handoff the next session can pick up, or one line in a shared log. From October 11 to 14, that log took 116 entries. And an agent saying "done" does not close anything. AXIOM closes a job only after it has checked the result against something real: the file, the page, the message record. If it can't check, the job stays open and says so. What this costs One door is slower for small things. A two-minute fix still goes through the front. It also means AXIOM is a single point of failure. If it routes badly or checks lazily, everything behind it inherits the mistake. That's the real risk in this design, and it's why the next two notes exist: where the agents are made to stop, and how they have to prove their work. Why it's worth it I train, I coach, I'm building a company. I'm often on my phone between sets. The point of the system is that I can say what I want once, put the phone down, and come back to one answer I can trust. That only works if there is one place the answer comes from.
